metadata.note: The St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern Railway — the Iron Mountain Route — and the principal passenger lines of its system, drawn as five routes: the St. Louis–Texarkana main line, the Fort Smith branch, the Bald Knob–Memphis branch, the White River Division (Carthage, Missouri–Newport, Arkansas) and the Louisiana Division (Little Rock–Alexandria, with the Alexandria–Lake Charles line). Each route appears as more than one feature because ownership changed: the 1858–1874 St. Louis and Iron Mountain Railroad, the 1874–1917 Iron Mountain, the 1879–1906 Little Rock and Fort Smith Railway and the post-1917 Missouri Pacific each carry their own company colour over identical geometry, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. This replaces the layer's previous single feature, which drew St. Louis–Texarkana on Amtrak's modern Texas Eagle GTFS alignment and kept Iron Mountain green through the 1917–1971 Missouri Pacific years.
metadata.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap, via route relations pulled from the OSM API and chained by shared node id, then simplified with Douglas-Peucker at 40 m. Relations used: 2214664 (UP De Soto Sub), 2210316 (Hoxie Sub), 2210320 (Little Rock Sub), 2210331 (Van Buren Sub), 2210321 (Memphis Sub), 2210333 (White Bluff Sub), 2209325 (McGehee Sub), 2209326 (Monroe Sub), 1456161 (Lake Charles Sub) and 6691528 (Missouri and Northern Arkansas Railroad, on the ex-MoPac White River line). Where these relations left gaps, extra ways were pulled by bounding box and filtered on old_railway_operator=MP. Every straight-line leg over 1 km is named in the feature's geometry_quality.
metadata.mileage_check: Traced against documented mileage: St. Louis–Pilot Knob 85.8 vs 86; St. Louis–Texarkana 485.3 vs ~490; Bald Knob–Memphis 88.4; Little Rock–Van Buren 155.5 (documented 165 to Fort Smith, ~9 mi of which is not drawn); Carthage–Newport 266.8; Little Rock–Alexandria 292.2; Alexandria–Lake Charles 98.0 vs ~92.
not_yet_sourced: No last-train date was found for the Little Rock–Monroe–Alexandria Louisiana Division or for the Alexandria–Lake Charles line. Both are drawn to 1965, a deliberately conservative cut-off; MoPac still ran two trains in 1969, so the true dates are probably later.
No last-train date was found for the Bald Knob–Memphis branch itself. It is drawn to 1965, when the Texas Eagle's Memphis section was discontinued.

Whether the Texas Eagle's Memphis section and the Memphis–Little Rock–Hot Springs locals ran over MoPac's own Bald Knob–Memphis rails, rather than over a connecting road, is not established by any source consulted here.

The build dates of the Arkansas segments of the Louisiana Division are not reconciled with the 1 Jul 1892 opening of through service to New Orleans; the Little Rock and Monroe Railway (1903) may have replaced part of the 1892 route.
The opening date of the Alexandria–Lake Charles line is not established; the feature is drawn from the Iron Mountain's 1 Sep 1909 purchase of the St. Louis, Watkins and Gulf.
Every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh in this layer is an estimate. None came from a timetable.

The Iron Mountain's other passenger routes are not yet drawn: the Belmont Branch (completed 14 Aug 1869), the Cairo and Fulton line from Bird's Point, the Illinois Division of the St. Louis Valley Railway, the Helena lines, the Hot Springs branch and the Kansas and Arkansas Valley into Indian Territory.
metadata.colour_note: St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern keeps #006747, the colour it already carried in this repo. NOTE: #006747 is also used by Kansas City Southern and by Southern Railway elsewhere in data/, and KCS's Southern Belle crosses this territory — three companies share the shade. That is a pre-existing clash, not one introduced here, but it is worth fixing. Missouri Pacific keeps #0057B8 from missouri_pacific_eagle.geojson. New here: #0E5C3F for the St. Louis and Iron Mountain Railroad and #4FA381 for the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railway.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>". Features added 2026-08-27 follow the same pattern (CLAUDE.md Rule 6).

properties.company: St. Louis and Iron Mountain Railroad
properties.line: St. Louis and Iron Mountain: St. Louis – Pilot Knob
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap: the St. Louis–Pilot Knob portion of UP's De Soto Subdivision (OSM relation 2214664), which is the original Iron Mountain alignment still in use. Traced length 85.8 mi against a documented 86 mi St. Louis–Pilot Knob. No approximated legs. The modern alignment is drawn for the 1858–1874 era; terminal trackage in St. Louis and around Pilot Knob has been rebuilt since, so the last mile at each end is later than the drawn era.
properties.speed_source: avg_speed_kmh is an estimate for 1860s–70s Missouri steam operation; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Chartered by special act of the Missouri legislature 3 Mar 1851; first dirt turned Oct 1853; built to bring ore north from Iron Mountain. Reached De Soto 1857 and was completed to Pilot Knob 2 Apr 1858. The state foreclosed 19 Feb 1866 and sold the road to Thomas Allen in Jan 1867; reorganised as the St. Louis and Iron Mountain Railroad 29 Jul 1867, seized again by the state Jan 1868 and returned that March. Consolidated with the two Cairo and Fulton companies on 6 May 1874 to form the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern. Headway is an estimate standing in for a few trains a day.
sources: Segment-level: opening date (2 Apr 1858), De Soto 1857, the 1866 foreclosure, the 1867 reorganisation and the 1874 consolidation all come from the Missouri Pacific Historical Society's chronology of the Iron Mountain.

properties.company: St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern Railway
properties.line: St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern: Iron Mountain Route
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, not the straight-line or Amtrak-GTFS approximation this feature previously carried. Assembled from UP's De Soto Subdivision (St. Louis–Poplar Bluff, OSM relation 2214664), Hoxie Subdivision (Poplar Bluff–Bald Knob–Little Rock, relation 2210316) and Little Rock Subdivision (Little Rock–Benton–Gurdon–Texarkana, relation 2210320, cut at Texarkana where the relation continues into Texas over the former Texas and Pacific). Traced length 485.3 mi against a documented ~490 mi St. Louis–Texarkana. The only approximated leg is a 0.47 km straight-line join through Poplar Bluff yard; the other four joins are under 10 m. This is the surviving alignment, so short relocations since 1917 (notably the Baring Cross crossing at Little Rock) are drawn as they are today, not as built. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 4 ruled segments totalling 82 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).
properties.speed_source: avg_speed_kmh is an estimate for a late-19th-century through train over this profile; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Formed 6 May 1874 by consolidating the St. Louis and Iron Mountain Railroad (1867) with the Cairo and Fulton Railroad companies of Missouri and of Arkansas. The Arkansas end had opened in stages: the first train from St. Louis reached Little Rock 7 Feb 1873, the Baring Cross bridge over the Arkansas River was finished 21 Dec 1873, the first through Little Rock–St. Louis train left 22 Dec 1873, and the Cairo and Fulton reached Texarkana 15 Jan 1874. The whole road was converted from broad to standard gauge in a single day, 28 Jun 1879. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1873–74 opening dates, the 6 May 1874 consolidation and the 28 Jun 1879 gauge change are from the Missouri Pacific Historical Society chronology.

segments.note: Jay Gould took control in 1880, and by Dec 1883 the Iron Mountain was part of a 9,547-mile Gould system; the road's notoriety was fixed by the Gad's Hill robbery of 31 Jan 1874 and the Olyphant robbery of 3 Nov 1893. Under Gould and his son the Iron Mountain became the system's south-western trunk, and from 5 Dec 1915 it carried the new St. Louis–San Antonio Sunshine Special. George J. Gould lost control 9 Mar 1915, the road entered receivership 19 Aug 1915, and it was merged into the Missouri Pacific 12 May 1917. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: Gould control, the 1883 system mileage, the 1915 receivership and the 12 May 1917 merger are from the MPHS chronology; the Sunshine Special's 5 Dec 1915 inauguration is from Bill Pollard's notes on MP passenger trains.

segments.note: The St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern was formally merged into the Missouri Pacific 12 May 1917, and this became MoPac's south-western main line. The Sunshine Special worked it from St. Louis to San Antonio and beyond, with a Memphis connection joining at Little Rock; the weekly all-Pullman City of Mexico ran St. Louis–Mexico City over it 1937–1940, scheduled non-stop from St. Louis to Little Rock. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 12 May 1917 merger is from the MPHS chronology; the Sunshine Special and City of Mexico operations over this line are from Bill Pollard's notes.

segments.note: The streamlined Texas Eagle was inaugurated 15 Aug 1948 and displaced the Sunshine Special to secondary trains 31–32. The Sunshine became a St. Louis–Texarkana train in 1954, lost its southbound half in summer 1955, and last appeared under its own name in the March 1961 Official Guide; its unnamed successor was consolidated into the Texas Eagle in Nov 1962. MoPac cut the Texas Eagle back over the 1960s — the El Paso section ended 31 May 1969 and the Texas intrastate portion 22 Sep 1970 — leaving a St. Louis–Texarkana train that ran until Amtrak took over on 1 May 1971. Amtrak's own Texas Eagle still uses this corridor; see amtrak.geojson. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 15 Aug 1948 Texas Eagle inauguration, the Sunshine Special's 1954–1962 decline and the 1969/1970/1971 end dates are from Bill Pollard's notes and the Wikipedia article on the MP Texas Eagle.

properties.company: Little Rock and Fort Smith Railway
properties.line: Little Rock and Fort Smith: Little Rock – Fort Smith
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap: UP's Van Buren Subdivision (OSM relation 2210331, ex-Missouri Pacific — the member ways carry old_railway_operator=MP) from Little Rock through Conway, Morrilton, Russellville, Clarksville, Ozark and Alma to Van Buren. Traced length 155.5 mi. Two approximated legs: a 2.44 km straight-line join at Russellville and a 1.86 km join at Alma, both where the OSM relation's member ways stop short of each other. DRAWN END IS VAN BUREN, NOT FORT SMITH: the documented route is 165 mi to Fort Smith, and the last ~9 mi — west into Oklahoma to the Moffett wye, then back east over the Arkansas River bridge into Fort Smith station — is abandoned and too fragmentary in OSM to trace, so it is not drawn. The line label still names Fort Smith because that is the route passengers bought.
properties.speed_source: avg_speed_kmh is an estimate for a branch-line local over this profile; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Chartered 25 Nov 1853 as the Little Rock and Fort Smith Branch of the Cairo and Fulton, renamed the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroad 22 Jan 1855 and sold at foreclosure to the bondholders 10 Dec 1874; the reorganised company became the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railway 12 Jun 1875. It had laid its first 24 miles west from Argenta (North Little Rock) by 1870 and 82 miles by 1871, and reached Van Buren 30 Jan 1879. Jay Gould bought the railway in 1887 and it was sold outright to the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern 13 Apr 1906. Drawn from 1879, when the line reached Van Buren; German immigrant settlement followed the tracks across the Arkansas River valley. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 30 Jan 1879 arrival at Van Buren, the 1870–71 construction figures and Gould's 1887 purchase are from the Encyclopedia of Arkansas; the charter dates and the 13 Apr 1906 sale are from the MPHS chronology.

segments.note: Missouri Pacific worked the former Little Rock and Fort Smith line from the 12 May 1917 merger. Trains 125–126 ran Kansas City–Little Rock–Fort Smith; steam power was still on them through the 1940s, and in 1943 MoPac installed CTC from the west switch at Van Buren through Greenwood Junction down to Fort Smith. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: trains 125–126 and the 1943 CTC installation are documented in the Condren/Marre photographic record of MP passenger trains at Fort Smith and Van Buren.

segments.note: Diesels (E7s, E8s and Alco PAs) took over trains 125–126 in the 1950s, working into Fort Smith over the Arkansas River bridge and the station wye. The last northbound Missouri Pacific passenger train stopped at Van Buren on 28 Mar 1960; the last Fort Smith round trip was 27 Mar 1960. Freight continued over the line, which is UP's Van Buren Subdivision today, but no scheduled passenger train has run since. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 27–28 Mar 1960 last trips are documented by dated photographs of trains 125 and 126 at Fort Smith and Van Buren in the Condren/Marre collection.

segments.note: Jay Gould's Bald Knob and Memphis Railroad was built 1886–1888 to give the Iron Mountain an east–west connection: Gould wrote a $1,500,000 cheque for its construction on 4 Jan 1887, and the branch reached the Mississippi opposite Memphis on 16 Nov 1887, opening through to Memphis in 1888. It met the main line at Bald Knob, where the Iron Mountain had arrived in 1872 and where the company put up a new depot in 1915. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1886–88 construction, Gould's 4 Jan 1887 cheque, the 16 Nov 1887 arrival at the river and the 1915 Bald Knob depot are from the Encyclopedia of Arkansas entry on Bald Knob.

segments.note: Missouri Pacific took over operation at Bald Knob in 1917. The branch carried the Memphis connection of the Sunshine Special, which joined the main train at Little Rock, and the St. Louis–Memphis Tennessean (1927–1948); Memphis–Little Rock–Hot Springs locals ran in two pairs. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the Memphis connection of the Sunshine Special and the Memphis–Little Rock–Hot Springs trains are described in Bill Pollard's notes; the Tennessean's 1927–1948 dates are from his list of MP name trains. Which physical route the Tennessean used between St. Louis and Memphis is not established here.

segments.note: From 15 Aug 1948 a section of the Texas Eagle split at Little Rock and ran east to Memphis. One of the two pairs of Memphis–Little Rock–Hot Springs trains was dropped in Jan 1962, and the Texas Eagle's Memphis section was discontinued in Aug 1965; by 1967 the Little Rock–Memphis connection had gone entirely. Freight continues over the line as UP's Memphis Subdivision. Headway estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the Aug 1965 end of the Texas Eagle's Memphis section is sourced, and the Jan 1962 cut of one Memphis–Little Rock–Hot Springs pair is sourced, but no source consulted here states that these trains ran over MoPac's own Bald Knob–Memphis rails rather than a connecting road, nor gives a last-train date for the branch itself. The 1965 end year is the best-supported figure, not a documented last run.

properties.company: St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern Railway
properties.line: St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern: White River Division
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap: the Missouri and Northern Arkansas Railroad route relation (OSM relation 6691528), which runs on the former Missouri Pacific White River line, cut at Carthage, Missouri at the north end and at Diaz/Newport, Arkansas at the south. Traced length 266.8 mi through Aurora, Branson, Hollister, Harrison, Flippin, Cotter, Calico Rock, Batesville and Diaz. No approximated legs. The White River dams flooded parts of the valley after 1950 and some of the line was relocated; the modern alignment is drawn throughout.
properties.speed_source: avg_speed_kmh is an estimate for a river-grade line with heavy curvature; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: The White River Railway was organised under Arkansas law 8 Feb 1901 and sold to the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern 31 Jan 1903. Construction began in Jan 1902, working north from Batesville — which the Iron Mountain's own White River extension from Diaz had already reached in 1883 — and south from Carthage, Missouri; the final spike went in 29 Dec 1905. Cotter, a 300-acre farm before the railway, was a boomtown of 600 people and 43 businesses by about 1905. Drawn from 1906, the first full year of through service. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 8 Feb 1901 organisation and 31 Jan 1903 sale are from the MPHS chronology; the Jan 1902 start, the two-ended construction from Batesville and Carthage, the 29 Dec 1905 final spike and the growth of Cotter are from the Mountain Home Observer's history of the White River Railway.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap: the Missouri and Northern Arkansas Railroad route relation (OSM relation 6691528), which runs on the former Missouri Pacific White River line, cut at Carthage, Missouri at the north end and at Diaz/Newport, Arkansas at the south. Traced length 266.8 mi through Aurora, Branson, Hollister, Harrison, Flippin, Cotter, Calico Rock, Batesville and Diaz. No approximated legs. The White River dams flooded parts of the valley after 1950 and some of the line was relocated; the modern alignment is drawn throughout.
properties.speed_source: avg_speed_kmh is an estimate for a river-grade line with heavy curvature; no timetable was consulted.

segments.note: Missouri Pacific worked the White River line from the 12 May 1917 merger, using it as its Kansas City–Arkansas route. Headway estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the 12 May 1917 merger is sourced, but no source consulted here documents the service pattern over this line between 1917 and 1931.

segments.note: The Southern Scenic ran the White River line between Kansas City and Memphis from 1931 to 1952, as a branch of MoPac's St. Louis–Denver–San Francisco Scenic Limited and carrying through cars between Memphis and Denver. It handled express and mail in Railway Post Office cars alongside its passengers. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the Southern Scenic's 1931–1952 Kansas City–Memphis operation over the White River line, and its RPO and express traffic, are from the Mountain Home Observer history; the 1931–1952 span also appears in Bill Pollard's list of MP name trains.

segments.note: After the Southern Scenic name disappeared in 1952 the line kept unnamed passenger service for eight more years. The last passenger train over the White River line ran 20 Mar 1960. Freight continued; the line passed to Union Pacific with the 1982 MoPac merger and is operated today by the Missouri and Northern Arkansas Railroad, but carries no scheduled passengers. Headway estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 20 Mar 1960 last passenger train, and the later MoPac–UP–M&NA succession, are from the Mountain Home Observer history of the White River Railway.

segments.note: The Iron Mountain's route south from Little Rock was assembled from purchased roads: the Little Rock, Mississippi River and Texas Railway (itself built on the Little Rock, Pine Bluff and New Orleans and the Mississippi, Ouachita and Red River) was deeded to the Iron Mountain by Gould 28 Jan 1887, and the Houston, Central Arkansas and Northern — which built south from the Arkansas–Louisiana line through Monroe to Alexandria, 145 miles completed in July 1892 — was sold to the Iron Mountain 13 Dec 1893 after a brief spell under the Alexandria and St. Louis Railway. Through service to New Orleans over the HCA&N opened 1 Jul 1892, which is where this line is drawn from. The Little Rock and Monroe Railway (organised 1903) and the Mississippi River, Hamburg and Western were added 1 Sep 1909. Headway estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the corporate dates (1887, 1892, 1893, 1909) come from the MPHS predecessor list and the 1892 HCA&N construction from msrailroads.com, but no source consulted here reconciles those dates segment by segment against the alignment drawn — in particular whether the Pine Bluff–Monroe portion drawn here is the 1892 route or the later Little Rock and Monroe Railway cut-off. Treat 1892 as the year through service began, not as a build date for every mile drawn.

segments.note: The Kansas City, Watkins and Gulf Railway, organised in Louisiana 7 Jun 1887, went into receivership 12 Feb 1898, was sold at foreclosure 24 Mar 1902 and reorganised 28 May 1902 as the St. Louis, Watkins and Gulf Railway. It was sold to the St. Louis, Iron Mountain and Southern on 1 Sep 1909, which is where this line is drawn from — the Iron Mountain's own outlet from Alexandria to the Gulf at Lake Charles. The date the line itself opened between Alexandria and Lake Charles was not established; 1909 is the date the Iron Mountain took it over, which is the conservative choice for this map.

segments.note: Missouri Pacific worked the former St. Louis, Watkins and Gulf from the 12 May 1917 merger. The Louisiana Sunshine Special ran Little Rock–Lake Charles over it, and as late as the 1950s the northbound Sunshine Special picked up a Lake Charles sleeper at Little Rock for St. Louis; that car moved to the Texas Eagle after 7 Mar 1961. Drawn to 1965 on the same conservative basis as the Louisiana Division.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the Louisiana Sunshine Special (Little Rock–Lake Charles) and the Lake Charles sleeper handed to the Sunshine Special at Little Rock until 7 Mar 1961 are sourced, but no last-train date for the Alexandria–Lake Charles line was found. 1965 is a conservative cut-off, not a documented discontinuance.
